title: Manas AI CEO: China and India Can Reverse Eroom's Law
summary: Manas AI CEO Siddhartha Mukherjee reveals how China and India's AI capabilities could reverse Eroom's Law and accelerate drug discovery at HTLS 2026.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Manas AI CEO Siddhartha Mukherjee declared China and India can reverse Eroom's Law, the pharmaceutical productivity decline trend.
- Speaking at HTLS 2026, Mukherjee highlighted how AI infrastructure in emerging markets accelerates drug discovery timelines dramatically.
- The announcement positions Asian markets as leaders in reversing the 60-year trend of rising drug development costs.


Manas AI CEO Siddhartha Mukherjee delivered a groundbreaking keynote at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit (HTLS) 2026, officially launched on November 14, 2026, declaring that China and India possess the AI infrastructure and talent to reverse Eroom's Law, the decades-long trend of declining pharmaceutical R&D productivity. The announcement marks a significant shift in the global drug discovery landscape, positioning emerging Asian markets as potential leaders in accelerating medical breakthroughs.


Eroom's Law, Moore's Law spelled backward, describes how drug discovery costs have doubled every nine years since 1950 while producing fewer new medicines. Mukherjee's thesis centers on how AI-driven computational biology and massive datasets in China and India can break this cycle.


## Officially launched on November 14, 2026


The HTLS 2026 conference, held in New Delhi, brought together global healthcare and technology leaders. Mukherjee's keynote session focused specifically on how Manas AI's partnerships with research institutions across China and India are demonstrating measurable reductions in drug discovery timelines. According to his presentation, AI models trained on Asian genetic datasets are identifying drug candidates 40 to 60 percent faster than traditional methods.


The timing coincides with both nations ramping up investments in computational infrastructure for life sciences research, creating what Mukherjee called a "perfect storm" for pharmaceutical innovation.


## Why China and India Hold Unique Advantages


Mukherjee outlined three core advantages these markets bring to reversing Eroom's Law. First, the sheer scale of genetic diversity in populations exceeding 2.8 billion people provides richer datasets for training AI models. Second, lower computational costs and engineering talent availability reduce the capital barriers that have historically constrained Western pharma R&D budgets.


Third, regulatory frameworks in both nations are evolving to accommodate AI-assisted drug discovery pathways, potentially shortening approval timelines. Mukherjee emphasized that these factors combined create conditions where the cost-per-discovery curve can finally bend downward after 70 years of climbing.


## Manas AI's Role in the Transformation


Manas AI, headquartered in Bangalore with research operations in Shanghai, has built proprietary AI platforms that analyze protein folding, molecular interactions, and clinical trial data at unprecedented scale. The company's work with academic medical centers in both countries has produced early-stage candidates for oncology and neurodegenerative diseases that reached preclinical milestones in 18 months versus the typical 3 to 5 year timeline.


Mukherjee revealed that Manas AI is expanding its collaboration network to include 12 additional research institutions across tier-two cities in India and provincial capitals in China, targeting disease areas where Western pharma has underinvested due to cost constraints.


## Industry Response and Skepticism


While Mukherjee's vision attracted attention at HTLS 2026, pharmaceutical industry analysts remain cautious. Critics point to regulatory uncertainties, data privacy challenges, and the reality that AI can accelerate discovery but not eliminate the biological complexity of clinical trials. Some Western executives privately question whether emerging markets can sustain the quality control standards required for globally marketable drugs.


However, several major pharmaceutical companies have quietly initiated exploratory partnerships with AI labs in both nations, signaling that Mukherjee's thesis is being taken seriously at the highest levels of the industry.


## What This Means


If China and India succeed in reversing Eroom's Law through AI-driven drug discovery, the implications extend far beyond faster timelines and lower costs. It would represent a fundamental shift in where pharmaceutical innovation happens, democratizing access to life-saving medicines and potentially rewriting the economic geography of the global healthcare industry. Mukherjee's HTLS 2026 keynote may be remembered as the moment this transition moved from theory to declared strategy, with measurable progress already underway in labs across both nations.
